reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive LIPA deficiency spanning a continuous spectrum from severe infantile Wolman disease to milder late-onset cholesteryl ester storage disease
Infantile Wolman disease presents in the first weeks of life with vomiting, diarrhoea, malabsorption, failure to thrive, marked hepatosplenomegaly and rapid deterioration
Adrenal enlargement with punctate calcification on imaging is a highly suggestive feature of the infantile form
Later-onset disease presents with hepatomegaly, transaminitis, hepatic steatosis and an atherogenic dyslipidaemia (high LDL, low HDL)
Diagnosis rests on low lysosomal acid lipase enzyme activity (readily measured on dried blood spot) confirmed by LIPA genetic testing
Enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant lysosomal acid lipase (sebelipase alfa) is the disease-specific treatment and is transformative in the infantile form
Supportive care includes nutritional support, lipid-lowering therapy and monitoring for hepatic fibrosis in the later-onset spectrum
reference.pathophysiology: Lysosomal acid lipase hydrolyses cholesteryl esters and triglycerides taken up by cells through lipoprotein endocytosis, releasing free cholesterol and fatty acids for cellular use. Complete or near-complete deficiency causes massive lysosomal accumulation of cholesteryl esters and triglycerides in liver, spleen, intestine, adrenal glands and macrophages, producing the fulminant multi-organ infantile Wolman phenotype; partial deficiency causes the slower cholesteryl ester storage disease phenotype. Impaired liberation of free cholesterol disrupts cholesterol homeostasis, driving compensatory synthesis and the characteristic dyslipidaemia, while progressive tissue storage leads to hepatic failure or, in milder disease, fibrosis and premature atherosclerosis.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of infantile hepatosplenomegaly with failure to thrive (e.g. Niemann-Pick, Gaucher)
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in the later-onset form
Cystic fibrosis or other causes of malabsorption in infancy
additionalInvestigations: Lysosomal acid lipase enzyme activity assay (dried blood spot or leucocytes)
LIPA molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Abdominal imaging for hepatosplenomegaly and adrenal calcification
Fasting lipid profile and liver function tests
Liver biopsy showing microvesicular steatosis and lipid-laden macrophages where needed
Growth, nutritional and cardiovascular risk assessment across the spectrum
redFlags: Rapidly progressive failure to thrive with hepatosplenomegaly in early infancy
Adrenal calcification with signs of adrenal insufficiency
Progression to hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis or portal hypertension
Premature cardiovascular disease from severe dyslipidaemia
reference.prognosis: Untreated infantile Wolman disease is almost uniformly fatal within the first months of life, whereas the later-onset form is more indolent; enzyme replacement therapy substantially improves survival and hepatic and metabolic outcomes across the spectrum.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis in infants by not measuring enzyme activity in unexplained hepatosplenomegaly and failure to thrive
Mislabelling later-onset disease as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease or familial hypercholesterolaemia
Overlooking adrenal insufficiency in the infantile form
Delaying enzyme replacement therapy in rapidly progressive infantile disease
references: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
